221.quote_or_event: “In that place where the lowly are cared for-there, the Blessings of Your Glance of Grace rain down.”
221.explanation: Guru Nanak closes this Siree Raag hymn by saying that God's grace falls precisely where the lowest and poorest are looked after.
221.tie_back: Valluvar defines true giving as giving to those who have nothing, and Guru Nanak locates divine favour exactly where the destitute are cared for.
221.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
221._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on care for the destitute, but the verse speaks of where grace descends rather than defining charity against a calculated exchange as the Kural does.

222.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself a guru or a spiritual teacher, while he goes around begging - don't ever touch his feet. One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
222.explanation: In this salok Guru Nanak rejects holy men who live by begging, however spiritual their title, and holds up instead the person who earns honestly and shares part of it.
222.tie_back: Like the Kural, which says taking is bad even if called a good path and giving is good in itself, Guru Nanak refuses to honour begging dressed up as religion and praises earning and giving.
222.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
222._accuracy_note: Close on both halves (receiving disparaged even under a pious name, giving praised), though the Kural's point about giving without hope of heaven is not stated; the second line also appears elsewhere in this edition.

223.quote_or_event: “His Blessings are so abundant that there can be no written account of them. The Great Giver does not hold back anything.”
223.explanation: Japji's twenty-fifth pauri praises God as the Great Giver whose gifts are beyond counting and who withholds nothing.
223.tie_back: The Kural praises the noble person who never says 'I have nothing' and gives anyway; Guru Nanak presents the ideal giver as one who holds nothing back.
223.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5, Japji Sahib, Pauri 25, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
223._accuracy_note: Partial: the verse describes God's limitless generosity, not a human giver's refusal to plead poverty, so the parallel works only as a model of ungrudging giving.

224.quote_or_event: “The Great Giver keeps on giving, while those who receive grow weary of receiving.”
224.explanation: In the third pauri of Japji Guru Nanak contrasts the tireless generosity of God with the limited capacity of those who receive.
224.tie_back: The Kural pictures a generous person whose discomfort at being asked ends in the asker's joy; Gurbani's image of the Giver who never tires of giving is the nearest Sikh picture of giving as glad and unforced.
224.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2, Japji Sahib, Pauri 3, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
224._accuracy_note: Next-best only: no Sikh text found in this session matches the Kural's psychology of the giver's pain dissolving at the sight of the asker's happy face; this verse shares only the theme of joyful, untiring giving.

225.quote_or_event: “Without this grain, time does not pass in peace. Forsaking this grain, one does not meet the Lord of the World.”
225.explanation: In a hymn that opens by calling those who give up food hypocrites, Bhagat Kabir insists that food sustains life and that abandoning it does not bring anyone to God.
225.tie_back: Valluvar ranks relieving hunger above the ascetic's power to endure it, and Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib likewise refuses to treat fasting and self-starvation as a path to God.
225.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 873, Raag Gond, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
225._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit with the Sikh rejection of ascetic fasting, but the hymn defends eating rather than explicitly praising those who feed the hungry, which is the Kural's emphasis.

226.quote_or_event: According to the Janamsakhi tradition recorded by Macauliffe, Guru Nanak visited Duni Chand, a millionaire of Lahore who flew a flag for every lakh of rupees he owned. The Guru gave him a needle to return in the next world; when Duni Chand realised that not even a needle could go with him, the Guru told him to give some of his wealth in God's name and feed the poor so that it would accompany him, and Duni Chand distributed his treasure.
226.explanation: The story teaches that wealth hoarded stays behind at death, while wealth used to feed the poor goes with the giver.
226.tie_back: The Kural names relief of the destitute's hunger as the proper place to deposit wealth, and the Guru's counsel to Duni Chand, feed the poor and your wealth shall accompany you, makes exactly that point.
226.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), Vol. 1, Life of Guru Nanak, Chapter XI, pp. 129-130 (paraphrase)
226._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one in moral, but it is hagiographic Janamsakhi material retold by Macauliffe rather than scripture, so it is scored below a canonical parallel.

227.quote_or_event: “The Siblings of Destiny meet together, and eat and spend, but these resources do not diminish; they continue to increase.”
227.explanation: Guru Arjan describes a treasure inherited from the Father that grows rather than shrinks as the community shares and spends it together.
227.tie_back: The Kural promises that the habit of sharing food keeps the fiery disease of hunger away; Guru Arjan likewise teaches that what is shared in common is never exhausted.
227.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
227._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the treasure here is primarily the spiritual wealth of the Name, read by analogy with the Sikh practice of sharing food (vand chhakna); the same verse is used elsewhere in this edition.

228.quote_or_event: “He hoards gold and silver, but this wealth is false and poisonous, nothing more than ashes.”
228.explanation: In the Dakhni Oankar Guru Nanak warns that the gold and silver a person piles up is false wealth that turns to ash.
228.tie_back: Valluvar mocks the hard-hearted who keep wealth only to lose it, and Guru Nanak says the same of hoarding: what is kept back is worthless in the end.
228.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 937, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
228._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the futility of hoarding, but the verse does not speak of the joy of giving that the Kural says misers never know.

229.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, those houses in which neither the Holy nor the Lord are served - those houses are like cremation grounds; demons dwell within them.”
229.explanation: Kabir says that a household which serves neither holy people nor God is as desolate as a cremation ground.
229.tie_back: The Kural calls eating alone to keep one's stores full more wretched than begging; Kabir likewise judges the closed, unsharing household as worse than poor, a place of death.
229.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1374, Salok Bhagat Kabir 192 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
229._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Kabir condemns the house without service and devotion rather than solitary eating specifically; this salok also appears in an earlier chapter of this edition.

230.quote_or_event: “Without meditating in remembrance on the Lord, one's life is like that of a snake. This is how the faithless cynic lives, forgetting the Naam, the Name of the Lord.”
230.explanation: Guru Arjan compares a life without remembrance of God to a snake's long but harmful life.
230.tie_back: The Kural says death becomes sweet when one can no longer give, measuring life by its usefulness; Guru Arjan likewise judges a long life empty of its true purpose as no better than a snake's.
230.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 239, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
230._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both say a life without its proper purpose is not worth having, but Gurbani's measure is remembrance of God rather than the capacity to give, and it does not speak of preferring death.
